newsitem.title: USA: Rain needed as U.S. Midwest soy begins to set pods.
newsitem.headline: Rain needed as U.S. Midwest soy begins to set pods.

text.p: Overly dry weather in the central U.S. Midwest is seen only stunting the growth of the soybean crop so far, but rains are desperately needed as more of the crop enters the critical pod setting stage, university agronomists said.

"The corn plant and soybean plant are at a point in time where operation under moisture deficiency is not in their best interest," said Gary Pepper, agronomist with the University of Illinois in Champaign.
"In the soybeans, a number are blooming and a considerable number are working to produce pods," he said.
In its latest crop report issued Monday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said 81 percent of the U.S. crop was blooming and 38 percent was setting pods as of Sunday.
A lack of moisture during the pod-setting stage can affect pod development and severe moisture stress can cause immature pods to abort, Pepper said.
In central Missouri, where moisture was also very short during the month of July, soybean plants are shorter than normal, said Bill Wiebold, agronomist at the University of Missouri in Columbia.
"We're only noticing that the beans are short," Wiebold said. "When the beans start setting pods, then we could see some very serious problems.
Forecasters disagree when the very dry areas including central Illinois, Indiana and Missouri could receive rain.
Many, however expect much of the Midwest to remain dry until the weekend, when much more of the soybean crop will be setting pods.

In Missouri, topsoil moisture was rated 23 percent very short, 49 percent short, 27 percent adequate and one per cent surplus for the week ended Friday, August 1, according to that state's latest crop report.
